edition.locus: Divine Institutes 3.19 (death's quality / eternal reward or penalty)

source_text: At illi qui de mortis bono disputant quia nihil ueri sciunt, sic argumentantur: si nihil est post mortem, non est malum mors; aufert enim sensum mali. si autem supersunt animae, etiam bonum est, quia inmortalitas sequitur. quam sententiam Cicero de Legibus sic explicauit: gratulemurque nobis, quoniam mors aut meliorem quam qui est in uita aut certe non deteriorem adlatura est statum: nam sine corpore animo uigente diuina uita est, sensu carente nihil profecto est mali. argute, ut sibi uidentur, quasi nihil esse aliut possit. atquin utrumque hoc falsum est. docent enim diuinae litterae non extingui animas, sed aut pro iustitia praemio adfici aut poena pro sceleribus sempiterna. nec enim fas est aut eum qui sceleratus in uita feliciter fuerit, effugere quod meretur aut eum qui ob iustitiam miserrimus fuerit, sua mercede fraudari. quod adeo uerum est, ut idem Tullius in Consolatione non easdem sedes incolere iustos atque inpios praedicauerit. nec enim omnibus inquit idem illi sapientes arbitrati sunt eundem cursum in caelum patere. nam uitiis et sceleribus contaminatos deprimi in tenebras atque in caeno iacere docuerunt, castos autem animos, puros integros incorruptos, bonis etiam studiis atque artibus expolitos leui quodam et facili lapsu ad deos id est ad naturam similem sui peruolare. quae sententia superiori illi argumento repugnat. illut enim sic adsumptum est, tamquam necesse sit omnem hominem natum inmortalitate donari. quod igitur erit. discrimen uirtutis ac sceleris, si nihil interest utrumne Aristides sit aliquis an Phalaris, utrum Cato an Catilina? sed hanc repugnantiam rerum sententiarumque non cernit nisi qui tenet ueritatem. si quis igitur nos roget utrumne bonum sit mors . an malum, respondebimus qualitatem eius ex uitae ratione pendere. nam sicut uita ipsa bonum est, si cum uirtute uiuatur, malum, si cum scelere, sic et mors ex praeteritis uitae actibus ponderanda est. ita fit ut si uita in dei religione transacta sit, mors malum non sit, quia translatio est ad inmortalitatem: sin aliter, malum sit necesse est, quoniam ut dixi ad aeterna supplicia transmittit. quid ergo dicemus nisi errare illos qui aut mortem adpetunt tamquam bonum aut uitam fugiunt tamquam malum? nisi quod sunt iniquissimi, qui pauciora mala non pensant bonis pluribus. nam cum omnem uitam per exquisitas et uarias traducant uoluptates, mori cupiunt, si quid forte iis amaritudinis superuenit, et sic habent, tamquam illis numquam fuerit bene, si aliquando fuerit male. damnant igitur uitam omnem plenamque nihil aliut quam malis opinantur. hine nata est inepta illa sententia, hanc esse mortem quam nos uitam putemus, illam uitam quam nos pro morte timeamus: ita primum bonum esse non nasci, secundum, citius mori. quae ut maioris sit auctoritatis, Sileno adtribuitur. Cicero in Consolatione non nasci inquit longe optimum nec in hos scopulos incidere uitae, proximum autem, si natus sis, quam primum tamquam ex incendio effugere fortunae. credidisse illum uanissimo dicto exinde apparet, quod adiecit de suo aliquid, ut ornaret. quaero igitur cui esse optimum putet non nasci, cum sit nullns omnino qui sentiat: nam ut bonum sit aliquid aut malum, sensus efficit. deinde, cur omnem uitam nihil esse aliud quam scopulos et incendium putauerit: quasi aut in nostra fuerit potestate ne nasceremur aut uitam nobis fortuna tribuat, non deus, aut uiuendi ratio quicquam simile incendio habere uideatur. non dissimile Platonis illut est, quod aiebat se gratias agere naturae: primum quod homo natus esset potius quam mutum animal, deinde quod mas potius quam femina, quod Graecus quam barbarus, postremo quod Atheniensis et quod temporibus Socratis. dici non potest quantam mentibus caecitatem, quantos pariat errores ignoratio ueritatis. ego plane contenderim numquam quicquam in rebus humanis dictum esse delirius: quasi uero si ant barbarus aut mulier aut asinus denique natus esset, idem ipse Plato esset ac non illud ipsum quod natus fuisset. sed uidelicet Pythagorae credidit, qui ut uetaret homines animalibus uesci, dixit animas de corporibus in aliorum animalium corpora commeare. quod et uanum et inpossibile est: uanum, quia necesse non fuit ueteres animas in noua corpora inducere, cum idem artifex qui primas aliquando fecerat, potuerit semper nouas facere, inpossibile, quia rectae rationis anima tam inmutare naturam status sui non potest quam ignis aut deorsum niti aut in transuersum fluminis modo flammam suam fundere. existimauit igitur homo sapiens potuisse fieri, ut anima quae tunc erat in Platone, in aliquod mutum animal includeretur essetque humano sensu praedita, ut intellegeret ac doleret incongruenti se corpore oneratam. quanto sanius faceret, si gratias agere se diceret, quod ingeniosus, quod docilis natus esset, quod in iis opibus, ut liberaliter erudiretur! nam quod Athenis natus est, quid in eo beneficii fuit? an non plurimi extiterunt in aliis ciuitatibus excellenti ingenio atque doctrina uiri, qui meliores singuli quam omnes Athenienses fuerunt? quanta hominum milia fuisse credamus qui et Athenis nati et temporibus Socratis indocti tamen ac stulti fuerint? non enim parietes aut locus in quo quisque est effusus ex utero, conciliat homini sapientiam. quid uero attinuit Socratis se temporibus natum gratulari? num Socrates ingenia discentibus potuit commodare? non uenit in mentem Platoni Alcibiaden quoque et Critiam eiusdem Socratis adsiduos auditores fuisse, quorum alter hostis patriae acerrimus fuit, alter crudelissimus omnium tyrannorum?
pass_a_gloss: Philosophers: death either no-evil (nothing after) or good (immortality). Both false—divinae litterae: souls get praemium for iustitia or poena sempiterna for scelera. Death's quality hangs on life: in dei religione → transfer to immortality; else eternal punishments. Attacks 'best not to be born' and Plato/Pythagoras reincarnation folly.
pass_b_english: But those who dispute about death's good, because they know nothing true, argue thus: if there is nothing after death, death is not an evil; for it removes sense of evil. But if souls survive, it is even a good, because immortality follows. Which opinion Cicero explained thus in the Laws: and let us congratulate ourselves, since death will bring a state either better than what is in life or at least not worse: for without body, with mind vigorous, there is divine life; with sense lacking there is certainly nothing of evil. Cleverly, as they think, as if nothing else could be. But both of these are false.

For the divine letters teach that souls are not extinguished, but are either visited with prize for justice or with everlasting penalty for crimes. For it is not right either that one who was criminal in life yet fortunate should escape what he deserves, or that one who was most wretched because of justice should be cheated of his wage. Which is so true that the same Tullius in the Consolation declared that the just and the impious do not inhabit the same seats. For not for all, he says, did those same wise men think the same course into heaven lies open. For they taught that those contaminated by vices and crimes are pressed down into darkness and lie in filth, but that chaste minds, pure, whole, uncorrupted, polished also by good studies and arts, by a certain light and easy gliding fly through to the gods—that is, to a nature like themselves.

Which opinion fights that earlier argument. For that was assumed as if it were necessary that every human born be gifted with immortality. What then will be the discrimination of virtue and crime, if it makes no difference whether someone is an Aristides or a Phalaris, a Cato or a Catiline? But this conflict of things and opinions is seen only by one who holds the truth. If therefore anyone asks us whether death is a good or an evil, we will answer that its quality hangs from the manner of life. For just as life itself is a good if it is lived with virtue, an evil if with crime, so also death is to be weighed from the past acts of life. Thus it happens that if life has been spent in God's religion, death is not an evil, because it is a transfer to immortality: but if otherwise, it must be an evil, since as I said it sends across to eternal punishments.

What then shall we say except that those err who either seek death as a good or flee life as an evil?—except that they are most unjust who do not balance fewer evils against more goods. For when they lead all life through sought-out and various pleasures, they desire to die if any bitterness happens to them, and so hold it as if it had never been well with them if it was ever badly. Therefore they condemn all life and think it full of nothing other than evils. Hence was born that foolish opinion, that this is death which we think life, that life which we fear as death: so that the first good is not to be born, the second to die sooner. Which, that it may have greater authority, is attributed to Silenus. Cicero in the Consolation: not to be born, he says, is by far best, nor to fall upon these reefs of life; but next, if you have been born, to flee as soon as possible as from fortune's fire.

That he believed that emptiest saying appears from this, that he added something of his own to adorn it. I ask therefore for whom he thinks it best not to be born, when there is no one at all who senses it: for that something be good or evil, sense makes it. Next, why he thought all life nothing other than reefs and fire: as if either it had been in our power that we not be born, or fortune rather than God grants us life, or the manner of living seems to have anything like a fire.

Not unlike is that of Plato, that he said he gave thanks to nature: first that he had been born a human rather than a mute animal, then a male rather than a female, a Greek rather than a barbarian, finally an Athenian and in Socrates' times. It cannot be said how much blindness to minds, how many errors ignorance of the truth bears. I would plainly contend that never has anything more delirious been said in human affairs: as if if he had been born a barbarian or a woman or finally an ass, that same Plato would be, and not that very thing which he had been born. But clearly he believed Pythagoras, who, that he might forbid humans to eat animals, said souls pass from bodies into other animals' bodies. Which is both empty and impossible: empty, because it was not necessary to lead old souls into new bodies, when the same craftsman who had once made the first could always make new; impossible, because a soul of right reason cannot change the nature of its standing any more than fire can press downward or pour its flame sideways in the manner of a river.

Therefore the wise human thought it could happen that the soul which then was in Plato might be shut in some mute animal and be endowed with human sense, so that it would understand and grieve that it was burdened with an unfit body. How much more sanely he would act if he said he gave thanks that he was born talented, teachable, in such means that he might be liberally educated! For that he was born at Athens—what benefit was in that? Or did not very many exist in other cities, men of excellent talent and learning, who one by one were better than all the Athenians? How many thousands of humans should we believe there were who, born both at Athens and in Socrates' times, were nevertheless unlearned and foolish? For neither walls nor the place in which each was poured from the womb wins wisdom for a human. And what did it matter to congratulate himself that he was born in Socrates' times? Could Socrates lend talents to learners? Did it not come into Plato's mind that Alcibiades also and Critias were constant hearers of the same Socrates, of whom the one was the fiercest enemy of the fatherland, the other the cruelest of all tyrants?
